newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan PM dissolves parliament for Oct 20 election.
newsitem.headline: Japan PM dissolves parliament for Oct 20 election.

text.p: Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday dissolved Japan's parliament and set October 20 as the date for general elections.

The elections for the 500-seat Lower House, the first since July 1993 polls ended 38 years of unbroken rule by the Liberal Democratic Party and ushered in an era of coalition government, have so far failed to excite an apathetic public.

Most analysts expect a record-low turnout for a heated but issue-free contest after weeks of wrangling between the LDP -- which Hashimoto now heads -- and its two smaller coalition partners over timing of the polls.

The focus is on whether the LDP, which regained the reins of power in 1994 in a coalition with the Social Democratic Party and New Party Sakigake, can capture a simple majority or will be forced to shop for new coalition partners.
Hashimoto urged his party to fight to give him a second term unfettered by the need to compromise with coalition partners.
"Although the LDP has been the biggest party over the last three years, we still don't have a simple majority," Hashimoto told a party gathering after he dissolved parliament.
Hashimoto is expected to pin his bid for a second term on an improving economy and his handling of a bitter dispute with the southern prefecture of Okinawa over U.S. military bases.
The opposition Shinshinto (New Frontier Party), headed by former LDP powerbroker Ichiro Ozawa, plans to attack the government for imposing an unpopular sales tax rise scheduled for next April.

Shinshinto, made of components of the reformist government that ruled briefly in 1993-94 before being tripped up by the LDP, will also offer a plan for a drastic overhaul of the tax system and to cut bureaucratic red tape.
To Shinshinto's chagrin -- and widespread public scepticism -- the LDP has adopted administrative reform as its election platform, making it hard for voters to compare platforms.
But Hashimoto's pep talk to the LDP on Friday offered a hint that he stands more for continuity than drastic change.
"We are heading for a storm of reform, and our politics, administration and social system must weather it," he told LDP legislators.

Analysts say the most likely way for the LDP, to survive in government -- given that it is unlikely to capture a simple majority -- is to forge a coalition with a smaller party with reformist credentials.
The Democratic Party, a new 40-strong group of defectors from the Social Democrats and Sakigake, which boasts maverick Health Minister Naoto Kan as one of its members, fits the bill, analysts say.

"Stagnation would come if the LDP gets a simple majority," said John Neuffer, a political analyst at Mitsui Marine Research. "The economy would like a strong plurality for the LDP, with Kan and the Democrats there to hold Hashimoto's feet to the fire on reform."
The polls will be the first under reforms enacted in 1994 to correct a gerrymandered system so as to make campaigning less costly and reduce dependence on political donations.
Under the new system, candidates will contest 300 seats in single-seat constituencies, with the other 200 seats decided through proportional representation.
